changes.before: Organize a guide with navigation, headings, tables, and meaningful landmarks.
changes.after: Help readers find a guide’s sections and understand a simple table.

before: A long guide needs ways to find information and understand how pieces relate. Use a main heading for the whole guide, section headings for its topics, and navigation links for shortcuts. Meaningful page regions are also called landmarks because assistive tools can help people move among them. Tables are for information whose rows and columns have relationships, such as each trail and its distance. They should not be used just to place unrelated page content side by side. A clear reading order helps both sighted readers and people listening to the guide.

This complete example gives a short guide a working in-page shortcut. ```html Bird guide
Bird list

Neighborhood birds

Birds near the pond

Look quietly from the path.

``` The #birds address finds id="birds". nav's aria-label names its purpose. One main marks the central content, h1 names the guide, and h2 names a topic inside it.

A table is built from nested elements. table wraps the whole thing. caption names what the table is about. tr means table row. th means header cell, which labels a row or column. td means an ordinary data cell. thead groups header rows; tbody groups the body rows. These tags describe relationships; a border alone cannot explain them. A table can have several cells in each row, and their order should match the header order. Close every cell before closing its row, then close the row group before closing table.

scope="col" on a th says it labels its column. scope="row" can mark a header for its row. The caption names the table as a whole, while column headers tell readers what each value means. “Name” and “Wingspan” explain separate columns. A person listening to a table may need the header repeated to understand a value, so use real th elements rather than bold ordinary cells. Simple scope-based headers are useful here; complex tables with multiple overlapping header groups need more careful relationships and testing.

Put this table inside the birds section from the first example. ```html
Bird wingspans
Bird Wingspan
Mallard 85 cm
Great blue heron 180 cm
``` The caption introduces the information. The first header applies to bird names, and the second applies to measurements. Each data row follows that same two-cell pattern. These example values are content, not code instructions.

Reading order comes from the document's structure. Keep headings, explanatory text, and the matching table together so the guide makes sense in order. Test navigation using Tab and Enter, and check that shortcuts lead to real sections. Use a screen reader to listen to the landmarks, headings, table caption, and column relationships. Automated checks can detect a th or caption, but they cannot prove the words are helpful or that every relationship makes sense. Avoid skipping heading levels merely to make a heading look smaller; CSS can change appearance without changing the outline.

For this guide, use a named nav whose Trail list link has href="#trails" and a real section with id="trails". Put the guide in one main, with h1 and h2 headings. Add a table caption and at least two th cells with scope="col", then supply data in matching columns. Explain the difference between the table's title and its column labels before building it. After the checks, review the whole reading order, use the keyboard shortcut, and listen with a screen reader. Passing structural checks is a starting point for that review.
after: A long guide needs a clear path through its information. Use headings for its topics and navigation links for shortcuts. Keep each explanation beside the information it describes.

This page fragment links to the guide’s bird section. ```html
Bird list

Neighborhood birds

Birds near the pond

Look quietly from the path.

``` The link’s `#birds` matches the section’s id. The h1 names the guide, and h2 names one topic. `main` marks the main content.

A table shows information in related rows and columns. `<table>` wraps it. `<tr>` makes a row. `<th>` labels a row or column, and `<td>` holds an ordinary value. Use tables for related data, not just to position page parts.
`<caption>` names the whole table. A header cell with `scope="col"` names its column. A header with `scope="row"` names its row. These labels help a reader understand what a value means.

Put this table inside the bird section. ```html
Bird wingspans
BirdWingspan
Mallard85 cm
Great blue heron180 cm
``` `thead` groups the header row. `tbody` groups the data rows. Each row puts the bird first and its wingspan second, matching the column headers.

Read the page from top to bottom. The headings, explanation and table should make sense in that order. Try its shortcut with Tab and Enter. If you use a screen reader, check that it can find the section and read the table’s caption and headers.

Put Trail guide inside one main area. Add a named nav with a Trail list link to `#trails`. Wrap the table in `<section id="trails">` with an h2. Add a table caption. Change Trail and Length into `<th scope="col">` cells. Keep Creek Loop and 2 km as the data row.

before: Add a nav element with an aria-label name. Inside it, link to the trails section with href="#trails".
Put the guide inside one main element. Use h1 for its title and h2 for the trails heading.
Give the table a title with caption.
Use th for each column heading and give each th scope="col".
Try the page using only the keyboard. Use a screen reader to check that it reads the table title and column headings.
after: Add the named nav and matching trails section inside main.
Add the section heading and table caption.
Use column headers for Trail and Length, then run the checks.
Try the Trail list shortcut with the keyboard.

before.question: A table has a caption but its two columns contain ordinary td cells only. A reader cannot tell what “85 cm” measures. What addresses that problem?
choices: Add a Wingspan th with scope="col" above that column
before.explanation: The column header supplies the meaning of each measurement. A caption names the whole table; borders do not label its columns.

after.question: A table shows 85 cm, but the column has no label. What explains the measurement?
choices: A caption that says only 85 cm.
A Wingspan header with scope="col" above the column.
after.explanation: A column header explains the values below it. The caption names the whole table.

before: A caption names the table; th names columns.
Give nav an aria-label and link to an existing id.
Use one main, h1 then h2, caption and scope="col".
after: Keep one h1 for Trail guide and use h2 for the trails section.
The caption names the table; the th cells name its columns.
The link needs href="#trails" and the section needs id="trails".

changes.before: Automated checks do not replace keyboard and screen-reader review.

project.title: A long-form guide
project.task: Build a trail guide with a working section shortcut and a clearly labeled table.
project.done_when: The named navigation reaches the trails section in one main area, and the table has a caption plus Trail and Length column headers.
